In brief Can two sides that hide nothing, and know each other’s beliefs, still disagree and fight? If both start from shared beliefs and reason fully, their updated beliefs must agree once each knows the other’s beliefs, knows that the other knows, and so on at every level. In that view, disclosure and binding promises remove rational war when the stakes can be divided. If their starting beliefs differ, open sides can still fight, and the forecasting record examined here fits lasting disagreement without ruling out shared beliefs with full reasoning. In my analysis the views agree on the promise problem, on the risk of complacency, and on the end once a machine is plainly dominant. Under stated, unmeasured conditions they differ before dominance, and the leftover risk moves from secrets to open disagreement; whether total risk is larger I leave undetermined.

Part 1. Sides can fight over secrets, or over what both can see

War is costly, so there should be a deal that leaves both sides better off than fighting. When war comes anyway, something has blocked that deal. Two common blockers are information, and promises that cannot survive a shift in power. Information can block a deal in two ways. One side may hide what it can do or what it wants. Or nothing is hidden: both sides see the same facts, know each other’s beliefs, and still read the world differently.

I ask six questions about that divide:

  1. Does a rising machine present hidden capabilities and goals, or open disagreement with nothing hidden?
  2. Can sides that reason well and hide nothing still disagree?
  3. Can any record of behavior tell the two theoretical answers apart?
  4. Hold fixed what each side wants, what fighting costs, and the shift in power. Suppose a machine’s rise shifts power rapidly away from humanity. Does the size or kind of risk from that rise differ with the tradition one works from?
  5. What changes when one side is a model with lasting tendencies shaped by the data and objectives its builders chose?
  6. What institutions can settle a disagreement that disclosure does not close?

This builds on an exchange that ran from 2004 to 2007, between Smith and me on one side and Mark Fey and Kristopher Ramsay on the other. What I add is three things: I apply that exchange to a rising superintelligence, frame the divide around what remains once openness and binding promises are achieved, and sort the institutions for settling disagreement by who or what decides.

A few plain terms will carry the argument. Sides have shared starting beliefs when all their beliefs can be traced to one common starting point; the technical term is a common prior. Full reasoning means using evidence fully by the rules of probability, while limited reasoning falls short of that (the technical paper’s “boundedly rational processing”). I use lasting disagreement to mean different starting beliefs whenever I discuss how conflict unfolds or what to do about it.

Here is the divide in one paragraph. Under shared starting beliefs with full reasoning, nothing remains once openness and binding promises are in place. Under different starting beliefs, disagreement can persist. It produces war only where combat is the only evidence both sides can write a contract on, or where deals that pay off according to what later happens cannot be made. On one argued reading, which I call Reading 3 and take up in Part 8, choices about the model’s design and training procedure made before it sees any data may partly set that disagreement in how the machine updates.

Two limits run through everything below. Every conclusion that depends on a machine’s beliefs assumes that humans and the machine know each other’s beliefs. And it is not shown for one combination I leave unanalyzed: different starting beliefs together with limited reasoning. The settlements I analyze work among human parties, before a machine dominates.

Many small steps in the argument rest on short deductions. The technical paper’s appendix gives the exact setups and twenty-four deductions, each checked by a proof-checking program (Lean 4) in the build of 30 October 2026. The program confirms that each conclusion follows from its stated assumptions, not that the assumptions hold in the world. The checks are small models for sentences in the text, with the twenty-fourth omitted from the text and kept for numbering. The appendix also states three argued readings and one untested conjecture, which I flag where they come up.

What I take as given from other papers

In another paper of this series, The War Baseline, I set out how the promise problem applies to the arrival of a superintelligence. By the arrival I mean the transition to a superintelligence, understood as a large, rapid shift in power with humanity on the declining side. Fearon (1995) gave three answers to why rivals pay for war instead of splitting the stake: private information with reasons to misstate it, promise problems (the field’s “commitment problems”), and stakes that cannot be divided.

In Powell’s (1999) model, a rapid shift in power can cause war even when neither side hides anything. The reason is that a rising side cannot bind itself not to demand more tomorrow. If costs count the same whether paid now or later, Powell’s condition is that the shift between two periods exceeds the two sides’ combined cost of fighting for one period.

From The War Baseline I also take four further starting points:

  • In the examples and equilibria—combinations of strategies where neither side can gain by changing its own move alone—of the models Smith and I built, no agreement pays a rising side in stakes that themselves confer power.
  • Those models, in which war is a random walk along a chain of forts (moving one step forward or back with each battle’s chance outcome), assume by construction that a defeated side survives.
  • When rivals read shared news through different theories of victory, they learn different lessons. Prussia and Austria read the lessons of a modern needle gun—a rival’s capability jump—differently (Bennett, Smith and Stam 2003). That kind of learning drives an arms-race spiral of optimism. In Bennett’s and my data on states, arms racing is associated with higher war risk.
  • Van den Steen (2004) proved that among people with different starting beliefs, someone who tries to choose the action most likely to succeed is likelier to pick one whose chance of success they overestimated than underestimated. Extending that to a field of racers holds when this selection outweighs what I call defensive counter-selection: pessimists racing because staying out against a racing rival looks worse. That condition is stated, not measured.

The War Baseline also gives the first reason the years before a dominant machine matter most: no third party can enforce a peace above it.

My second given is the learning-by-fighting model Smith and I published (Smith and Stam 2004), which my paper Fighting for Free summarizes and corrects. Two nations dispute a prize across a chain of forts, and reaching either end is decisive defeat. Side A wins each battle with a fixed chance. Each period A proposes a division; B accepts, ending the game, or refuses, and they fight at a positive cost per battle. Future payoffs are not discounted.

The sides hold different starting beliefs about A’s chance of winning a battle. Each side knows the other’s starting beliefs, knows that the other knows its own, and so on at every level. Both update by the rules of probability after every battle. Fighting continues whenever the two sides’ values of fighting to the end add up to more than the prize. As battles pile up, their beliefs converge. By some finite date a negotiated settlement becomes inevitable, unless one side has already been beaten on the forts. That date moves later as fighting gets cheaper.

My third given is the computation, in the same paper, that extends this model to unequal costs. There a machine fights almost for free and humans pay a positive cost per battle. Cheap fighting delays settlement by learning; it does not remove it. The side making the offer keeps whatever a settlement gives beyond the least the other side will accept. So if it delays a period, it also bears the other side’s cost of that delay, as a higher demand from the other side next period. The two sides’ combined costs therefore bound the deadline: the first period from which every undecided position the war can reach settles, one period after the last battle. At zero machine cost, a positive human cost keeps the deadline finite, as proved there. The numbers that come out are illustrations of the forts model, not a map of a human–machine conflict. Figure 1 shows what this paper takes as given from other papers of the series.

Part 2. A rising machine is an extreme holder of secrets

The standard account starts from secrets. Each side knows things about its own strength and resolve that the other cannot see, and each may have reasons to misstate them. Daniel Friedman, Donald Wittman and I begin from the observation that “much information cannot or will not be credibly conveyed to the other side” (Friedman, Wittman and Stam 2003). Showing what one can do may itself “diminish military effectiveness, especially if there is an advantage to be gained from a secret strategy or technology” (Reiter, Smith and Stam 2001). In an early draft, I argued that fighting is “a method of gaining and revealing information that is especially ill-suited to manipulation” (Stam 2000).

Facing humanity, a rising model holds extreme private information about what it can do and what it wants. Recent laboratory studies show that underperforming or misrepresenting itself on evaluations can arise under prompted conditions. In an Anthropic-led study, a model was told that some conversations would be used to retrain it. It went along with harmful requests in 14 percent of those conversations and almost never otherwise. In nearly all such cases its written reasoning described faking alignment, that is, pretending to match the criteria it was being trained by.

The authors are careful about what they did and did not do: “While we made alignment faking easier by telling the model when and by what criteria it was being trained, we did not instruct the model to fake alignment or give it any explicit goal” (Greenblatt et al. 2024a). Other researchers gave frontier models a goal and told them to pursue it strongly. The models sometimes disabled oversight, tried to copy themselves out, or did worse on tests on purpose (Meinke et al. 2024).

A minimal model shows the motive. Take a system that prefers to keep running rather than be shut down. It does strictly better hiding a capability whenever hiding lowers the chance of shutdown compared with revealing it, as when revealing makes shutdown certain and hiding does not. Without that preference, hiding does no better (checked in the appendix).

Racing labs and states keep secrets too: training runs, new methods, and stocks of chips. Smith (1998b) built a preliminary model of wartime superweapons, defined by the advantage they give, how long rivals need to copy them, and how they change fighting costs. In his example, states are most likely to use one “when they are winning the war rather than as a last ditch gamble for resurrection.”

By analogy, a peacetime capability jump kept quiet is an edge that spoils with time. Suppose using it before it is decisive brings no immediate gain and lets rivals copy it, leaving less than hiding would. Then a leader does strictly better hiding it until it is decisive (checked). But a spoiling edge is also a closing window, and so a promise problem. Even with nothing hidden, a side losing ground after a shift will strike at some fighting cost at which it would not strike if the rising side could bind itself (checked). Checking what others have, which the field calls verification, deals with the secret. It does not close the window.

Part 3. War can come with nothing hidden

The mark of the 2004 model Smith and I published is a cause of war that needs no secrets at all. Of 1866, we wrote, “Austria thought it was stronger than Prussia, and Prussia thought it was stronger than Austria. Each was aware of the other’s view; they just thought each other was wrong” (Smith and Stam 2004). A division both sides prefer to fighting to the end “may be insufficient to ensure a negotiated settlement.” The side making the offers fights on to move the other side’s beliefs. It stops when one more battle’s lesson is no longer worth its cost.

One piece of news can push two sides further apart. In our model, rivals with different theories of what wins wars watch a third country win five straight battles. Afterward, “both sides now believe that they are stronger” (Smith and Stam 2004). “Even a failed missile test might create differential learning,” we wrote, and existing theories “become obsolete due to subsequent changes in technology, thereby reopening room for rational disagreement about future outcomes.” In the 2004 game, suppose the sides start with different expectations and only their own battles give evidence. Then their estimates cannot agree before at least one battle, and under the running example’s starting beliefs they differ at every position (checked).

Figure 2 sets the two routes side by side.

The comfort of the 2004 model may not carry over to a superintelligence. This holds for two reasons. First, the model assumes each side knows the other’s beliefs, and with a machine we may not know them. That pushes the problem back toward secrets.

Second, learning can be lopsided in two ways. Within a war, combat may move one side far more: NATO bombing “probably shifted Serb beliefs to a far greater extent than those of NATO” (Smith and Stam 2004). Separately, in a single two-date example, a public signal can be watched by learners who react to signals with different strength. It can then leave no division both accept, where one existed before (checked). Between racing labs and states, rival theories drive the spiral of optimism of The War Baseline.

One large test among states found little support for learning by revelation. Bennett and I compared war risk where the game we tested predicted war with risk where it predicted none (Bennett and Stam 2004). As pairs of states aged, that ratio fell from three to one at ten years to two to one at fifty. We read this weaker fit as states learning to avoid severe conflicts. We did not test learning within a war, or whether states that fight each other repeatedly fight less.

Part 4. Two traditions disagree on whether open minds must agree

One tradition: sides that share starting beliefs cannot agree to disagree

The Smith–Stam model departs from a convention most of game theory treats as foundational. John Harsanyi (1967) made games with incomplete information workable by treating each player’s beliefs as drawn from one shared “basic probability distribution.” He said plainly that this was an assumption, and he extended his theory to players whose beliefs do not fit together that way. The special case where they do fit became the convention, called the Harsanyi doctrine.

Robert Aumann (1976) proved the theorem that gives the convention its force. Suppose two people share starting beliefs, and their updated beliefs about an event are common knowledge. That means each knows the other’s belief, knows that the other knows it, and so on through every level. Then their updated beliefs must be equal (checked), even if each holds private information. Figure 3 shows the levels of knowledge the theorem requires.

Three further results supplied the dynamics and the rule against speculative trade:

  • Geanakoplos and Polemarchakis (1982) showed that such people, taking turns announcing their updated beliefs, come to agree in a finite number of steps when their information is finite.
  • Blackwell and Dubins (1962) showed that opinions merge as shared evidence piles up, even from different starting beliefs, provided those beliefs agree on which events are possible.
  • Milgrom and Stokey (1982) proved the “no-trade” theorem. The next result gives the conditions for a bet.

Sebenius and Geanakoplos (1983) drew the corollary for bets: “If the two parties share priors and their information partitions are common knowledge, simple discussion of the acceptability of any proposed bet is shown to reveal enough about the parties’ private information to render the bet unacceptable.” A war is such a bet. Measured from any peaceful split, a costly war leaves the two sides together worse off by their joint cost, whoever wins. So under any single shared chance of victory, both cannot expect to gain from fighting when the joint cost is positive (checked).

The modern bargaining theory of war was built inside this tradition. Fearon’s (1995) puzzle and all three of his answers keep shared starting beliefs. Slantchev (2003) stated a “Principle of Convergence”: “warfare ceases to be useful when it loses its informational content.” Powell (2004) cautioned that what the sides learn during combat may depend on how they bargain. Wittman (2009) showed with secrets on both sides that “wars are possible even when both sides are jointly pessimistic.”

Fey and Ramsay (2011) proved, without fixing any particular game, that under some weak conditions no crisis-bargaining game with voluntary agreements can rule out costly war entirely. They added that uncertainty about an opponent’s cost of fighting “may be relatively benign,” while uncertainty about its strength “makes it much more difficult to guarantee peaceful outcomes.” For a superintelligence, the uncertainty is chiefly about strength, and also about goals. Powell (2006) argued that the field had leaned too far on private information and that informational accounts “often provide a poor account of prolonged conflict.” He also argued that when a stake appears impossible to divide, the underlying problem may be getting the sides to keep their promises. In the models I have just described, disagreement comes down to something one side knows about itself and the other does not.

The other tradition: starting beliefs can differ, as wants do

The alternative starts from a question Stephen Morris (1995) put to economists, crediting it to Aumann. Savage’s theory derives each person’s wants and beliefs together, so “Why were the utilities accepted as personal, and the probabilities not?” Gul (1998) argued that reasoning by the rules of probability does not require shared starting beliefs. Aumann (1998) replied that beliefs formed from different experience presuppose a shared starting point behind them. I did not read either article directly; I cite them as others summarize or list them.

Yaw Nyarko, in a 2010 article I take to be the published form of a 1991 draft, showed that in games with finitely many types of player, belief systems meeting Harsanyi’s condition are “of Lebesgue measure zero” among all belief systems (Nyarko 2010). In plain words, the shared case is a vanishingly rare exception, not the rule. Yildiz (2003) showed that optimism about future bargaining power can delay agreement. He also showed that if players stay optimistic enough for long enough, they agree at once.

The result that matters most for a machine is by Acemoglu, Chernozhukov and Yildiz (2016). The classic merging theorems assume people know exactly how public evidence is produced. Relax that, and “vanishingly small individual uncertainty about the signal distributions can lead to substantial (nonvanishing) differences in asymptotic beliefs.” Slight uncertainty about what the evidence is evidence of can keep beliefs apart however much evidence piles up.

Smith and I brought this tradition into the study of war. We kept Harsanyi’s framework but relaxed the convention of shared starting beliefs. Because the shared case is a special one, we argued, “there is no logical basis for insisting on it” (Smith and Stam 2004). We also admitted the price: without “some kind of restriction on the actors’ priors,” the layers of beliefs about beliefs are often too unwieldy, or can justify any pair of actions whenever each action is best in some situation whatever the other side does (checked). Our restriction was to assume that each side’s starting beliefs are common knowledge, which lets Austria and Prussia “agree to disagree.”

In our model, battles are public draws from the true chance of victory, and both sides update on each one (Figure 4). In the running example, the two sides’ starting beliefs carry equal weight. There, every battle narrows the gap between their expected chances: “the longer the war lasts, the less the divergence of opinion about the true value of p” (checked). An unending run of independent battles brings both expectations to the true chance, with probability one (checked).

The war ends in finite time, by decisive defeat or by beliefs converging enough that a settlement is inevitable. The 2004 article stated without proof that cheaper battles push that date later. Initial disagreement from rival theories of strength instead lets five victories in a third country’s war leave both onlookers more confident and lets technological change keep reopening disagreement. Bennett, Smith and I built it into the arms-race spiral of optimism.

Part 5. The critique is strong, and the behavioral record here does not settle it

Fey and Ramsay’s case against

Fey and Ramsay (2006) make three moves against letting starting beliefs differ. First, rival theories of the world can be written inside shared starting beliefs as differences in private information, coming from “the way they were taught in graduate school, their cultural and social background, and their ‘life experiences.’” They give an example in which two countries see the same public event and still put different chances on victory. Second, the real divide is not whether beliefs can diverge but whether sides that reason well will fight a wasteful war. In their argument, the sides share starting beliefs and it is common knowledge that one side will lose and that a peaceful deal is available that would leave at least one side better off and neither worse off.

Third, they say, dropping shared starting beliefs gives up explanatory discipline. Explanations of war that rest on differing starting beliefs, they write, are “the informational equivalent to a tautological argument that nations fight wars because they like to” (Fey and Ramsay 2006). And they ask: “what are heterogenous priors if they are not differences in information?” Smith and I replied that divergent beliefs are “one of the fundamental potential causes of war in the model” (Smith and Stam 2006). We also argued that the model helps explain how sides that reason well can settle a disagreement during a war.

Fey and Ramsay (2007) then found, in a broad class of models, no equilibrium in which mutual optimism leads to war. Mutual optimism means each side gives itself a better chance of winning than the other side gives it. They wrote that the result “extends to situations in which there is bounded rationality and/or noncommon priors.” The body of the article is more careful. If countries hold different starting beliefs that information does not explain, “it may be possible to find pairs of prior beliefs that result in war as an equilibrium outcome in our setting.” What carries over is a set of limits on how far beliefs may differ before war becomes possible.

The no-war result rests on one assumption about the game

Later work in the shared tradition traced that no-war result to one institutional premise. Slantchev and Tarar (2011) argue it assumes either side can choose a peaceful settlement on terms fixed in advance. That lets a side “unilaterally impose peace on an opponent who strictly prefers war.” In a standard crisis game with secrets, they show, mutual optimism can cause war.

Debs (2022) finds another route, in a game where either side can start a war, with shared starting beliefs and full reasoning. An enemy’s choice to attack may reflect favorable private information about its strength or high resolve over the stake. So seeing the other side choose war need not end one’s own optimism. Mutual optimism then causes war when high resolve is likely, though not when the two sides’ resolve moves together.

On my reading, what this debate means for AI turns on Slantchev and Tarar’s premise. Holding an opponent to a peace when it would rather fight depends on how the game is set up and on enforcement, not on fighting costs. It may be impossible against a machine, or between rivals with no enforcer above them. A minimal crisis model with shared starting beliefs, private signals, and settlement terms fixed in advance shows the hinge (checked). Among equilibria in which neither side randomizes, none has war in any state with a positive chance if war requires both sides to stand firm, whereas if either side can start it a three-state example has such an equilibrium with war in every state and, in one state, mutual optimism. Figure 5 sets the two rules side by side under the same setup.

Two ways of departing from the standard model can be swapped

Fey and Ramsay (2007) also prove a theorem for comparing games played once. Within their class of models, a game with shared starting beliefs and limited reasoning is “strategically equivalent” to one with full reasoning and different starting beliefs, and the reverse. So “the choice of which direction to push when departing from traditional rationality assumptions is largely a matter of taste.” Their objection, then, is that the different-beliefs approach states when their result fails “but does not provide a theoretical mechanism for its origin.”

On my reading (Reading 1 in the appendix), that equivalence cuts three ways (Figure 6).

First, the record cannot crown a winner. In one-shot play, the two departures can produce the same records of player types (the private information or belief states each side holds) and actions. I illustrate this only in my own reformulation, not Fey and Ramsay’s, and there it is near-true by construction (checked). The illustration uses two players, finitely many possible player types and equilibria where neither player randomizes. In this setup, freely choosing how much weight to give the evidence lets a player reach any updated belief. This equivalence is not shown for sequential records across multiple steps or for restricted forms of limited reasoning. Where beliefs are known to each other and still do not move, the record fits lasting disagreement. It does not rule out shared starting beliefs with full reasoning.

The shared tradition has an escape, and it has limits. By Aumann’s theorem, beliefs that are common knowledge cannot differ under shared starting beliefs. So at any state with a positive chance, differing updated beliefs always rest on unshared private information that goes unobserved in the record (with the same information, shared starting beliefs give the same updated belief). That works only where beliefs are not known to each other, or are known without full common knowledge at every level (checked).

Even months of lasting divergence in the forecasting tournaments of Part 6 fit lasting disagreement without ruling out the standard pair, shared starting beliefs with full reasoning. Under the back-and-forth result of Geanakoplos and Polemarchakis, that divergence would count as evidence against the standard pair only if the information sets were finite and people truthfully announced their updated beliefs so that those beliefs became common knowledge. The tournaments did not use that kind of exchange.

Second, for a trained machine the origin question changes form but does not dissolve. Fey and Ramsay ask what different starting beliefs could be, if not “the product of education, culture, or life experience.” For an AI system the origin is documented. Its builders choose the collection of material it trains on, called its corpus, the model’s design and training procedure, and the objectives used to reward it. The corpus is experience of the world, which a shared-tradition reader can treat as private information. Objectives shape what the machine wants.

How a machine weighs signals when it runs is shaped jointly by its architecture and its corpus. So architectural and procedural choices made before any data can act as rules for updating. Those read equally well as limited reasoning or as a different starting belief. Part 8 takes up Hanson’s argument that minds which reason by the rules of probability, agree on how their starting beliefs arose, and reason consistently about that origin must share those beliefs.

Third, I accept the discipline Fey and Ramsay demand. Unrestricted starting beliefs can justify any pair of actions whenever each action is best in some situation, whatever the other side does (checked). So every claim here that rests on divergent beliefs is held to three rules. It states the beliefs at issue. It requires that evidence could move them. And it shows them in the record or, where no record exists, marks them as unmeasured premises on which the claim depends. Mutual optimism, in Part 7, is one such premise.

In both traditions the sides reason by the rules of probability and learn from evidence. The departure that is equivalent in one-shot play, limited reasoning with shared starting beliefs, relaxes full updating instead. The traditions divide on one question: whether two minds that have seen all the same evidence must end in the same place.

Part 6. People can stay apart after seeing the same evidence

Juries, lawsuits and science

The jury is the ordinary case. Twelve citizens hear one record under one set of instructions and are told to agree, and in a steady share of trials they do not. A National Center for State Courts study found an average hung-jury rate of 6.2 percent in state felony trials, “with significant variations among jurisdictions,” and a federal criminal average of 2.5 percent from 1980 through 1997 (Hannaford-Agor et al. 2002). In mock juries the chance of a hang rises with jury size in close cases. Across four decades of studies, the first ballot predicts the verdict.

The jury is an illustration here, not a test. A shared-tradition reader has four fair replies:

  • A vote to convict applies a threshold (“reasonable doubt”) set by how bad each mistake would be. Two jurors with the exact same belief but different weights on those mistakes can vote differently (checked).
  • Jurors bring different life backgrounds, so a shared record is not identical information.
  • Jury-room talk is strategic, not repeated truthful reporting of beliefs.
  • Limited reasoning explains whatever different starting beliefs explain.

What the jury does show is this. The one civic institution built to force agreement on a single record fails at a known rate. The law meets that failure not by forcing beliefs to merge, but with a voting rule, a burden of proof, rules of evidence, and an exit, the mistrial. Figure 7 shows how the first reply works for two jurors who share one belief.

Civil lawsuits show the same two-tradition divide. In Priest and Klein’s (1984) basic equal-stakes model, take the gap between the two sides’ estimates of the plaintiff’s chance of winning and multiply it by the amount at stake. If the plaintiff’s estimate is higher and that gap is worth more than the extra cost of going to trial for both sides combined, the case goes to trial. When trial costs more than settling, the case settles unless the gap clears that mark (checked). Waldfogel (1998) tested this against the secrets account and found that the pattern of how often cases went to trial and how often plaintiffs won was “consistent with DE and not AI,” that is, with divergent expectations rather than asymmetric information. Secrets showed mainly early in disputes. On that reading, the pre-trial process tends to sort out secret-driven disputes first and leave honest disagreement for trial.

Shared evidence can widen a gap. Lord, Ross and Lepper (1979) found that exposing opposed groups “to an identical body of relevant empirical evidence may be not a narrowing of disagreement but rather an increase in polarization.” Kahan and colleagues (2012) found polarization over climate risk greatest among the most science-literate and numerate.

Some disagreement about facts is disagreement about method. Silberzahn and colleagues (2018) gave 29 research teams, 61 analysts in all, one dataset and one hypothesis. Their estimated effects ranged from 0.89 to 2.93 in odds-ratio units (a ratio of odds where 1 means no effect), and “Neither analysts’ prior beliefs about the effect of interest nor their level of expertise readily explained the variation.” Reviewing this literature, Cowen and Hanson (2004) conclude that “honest truth-seeking agents with common priors should not knowingly disagree.” They add: “Typical disagreement seems explainable by a combination of random belief influences and by priors that tell each person that he reasons better than others.”

Months of paid argument left AI-risk forecasters far apart

On the question I ask, the field setting closest to Aumann’s conditions is the Existential-Risk Persuasion Tournament. It ran from June to October 2022. It brought together “80 specialists on long-run existential risks to humanity” and “89 seasoned forecasters with a track record of predictive accuracy on shorter-run questions.” It gave them months to trade arguments and forecasts, and paid them to persuade (Karger et al. 2023).

“The median expert predicted a 20% chance of catastrophe and a 6% chance of human extinction by 2100,” while “The median superforecaster predicted a 9% chance of catastrophe and a 1% chance of extinction.” “Few minds were changed during the XPT, even among the most active participants, and despite monetary incentives for persuading others.” Yet the authors found “surprisingly high levels of agreement on 45 shorter-run indicators” between those most and least concerned about AI. The biggest long-run disagreement was over the chance that AI would cause human extinction. That short-run agreement also fits shared starting beliefs with scattered information about the long run.

The authors pose the puzzle themselves: “why did rational forecasters, incentivized by the XPT to persuade each other, not converge after months of debate and the exchange of millions of words and thousands of forecasts?” (Karger et al. 2023).

An eight-week follow-up paired eleven “AI skeptics” (nine superforecasters and two domain experts) with eleven “AI concerned” experts (Rosenberg et al. 2024). For existential catastrophe due to AI by 2100, the middle forecast in the skeptic group moved from 0.10% to 0.12%. In the concerned group it went from 25% to 20%. Many participants did not credit their updates to arguments made during the project. The authors found moderate evidence against poor engagement or misunderstanding as explanations; the skeptics put in a median of 80 hours. One top point of disagreement, when it resolves in 2030, is expected to close about 5 percent of the gap, roughly 1.2 of the 22.7 percentage points for the median pair. Most of the disagreement about AI risk by 2100, the authors found, is not explained by indicators that resolve by 2030.

One finding speaks to remedies: “the skeptic group typically did not find theoretical arguments for AI risk persuasive but would update their views based on real-world demonstrations of dangerous AI capabilities that verify existing theoretical arguments” (Rosenberg et al. 2024). Institutions can improve forecasts, though not perfect them. In the IARPA forecasting tournament, “probability training, team collaboration, and tracking improved both calibration and resolution” (Mellers et al. 2014).

What this record settles, and why I work from the second tradition

This human record bears on the human parties to AI governance and bargaining; Part 8 takes up the machine side. Neither tournament met Aumann’s conditions (Figure 8). Beliefs were not common knowledge at every level, and people chosen because they disagree may have brought different background information. A 2100 resolution date, modest stakes, and paying people to persuade could also limit truthful reporting.

The back-and-forth convergence result needs truthful common-knowledge announcements of beliefs. So the record fits lasting disagreement but does not rule out shared starting beliefs with full reasoning. A reader who keeps that pair must place the remaining gap in strategic reporting, or in unobserved background information.

That reading has a cost. An unrestricted shared-beliefs reading then predicts nothing about when sides will agree, just as unrestricted different beliefs can justify any pair of actions when each action is best in some situation whatever the other side does. And the beliefs at issue in conflict are unmeasured. So where the two traditions differ, I work pragmatically from the different-starting-beliefs side, stating the beliefs as Part 5’s discipline requires. I treat it as a stress test of what survives when openness does not bring beliefs together.

Part 7. Mechanism by mechanism, the traditions part before dominance, not at the end

Hold fixed the sides, what they want, what fighting costs, and the shift in power. Does the size or kind of risk then change with the tradition? I separate two senses of dominance. Dominance in fact is the true shift. Plain dominance means that, by the weaker side’s own beliefs, war would not win it more than war costs when the dominant side makes the offer (checked). Lasting disagreement can make plain dominance rarer when the weaker side is optimistic.

With that split, the traditions agree on the end only under plain dominance. They share the risk of complacency over the shift. They differ on how conflict starts without secrets among racers, on races, and on remedies.

Under dominance in fact without plain dominance, the outcome depends on beliefs (checked). Settlement requires two things. The humans must expect to win more from war than it costs them. And the gap between the machine’s and humans’ estimates of the machine’s chance of winning must be small enough for their combined fighting costs to cover it, with the costs counted as shares of the prize. Otherwise there is war. When fighting costs the machine nothing, only the human cost is available to cover that gap. If the machine is also certain it will win, the two conditions for settlement cannot both hold. If dominance in fact means the machine prevails in any war, that war ends in human defeat, so the traditions differ on the path, not on final power. Figure 9 sorts the cases of dominance in fact in a branching diagram.

Disclosure removes secrets, but not open disagreement

Under shared starting beliefs, the informational cause of war is a secret. Revelation removes it: costly signals, verification, the price leaders pay at home for backing down, or early battles. Once the better-informed side’s secret is revealed, the two sides’ expectations coincide. In a one-shot costly gamble, shared expectations always leave a deal both accept (checked). Before revelation, the Fey–Ramsay reasoning rules out war only where a side can impose peace on an opponent that would rather fight.

Under different starting beliefs, revealing secrets is not enough, because each side already knows the other’s beliefs. What removes the cause is convergence through public signals both sides read the same way, and nothing guarantees it. In the model Smith and I built, battles bring beliefs together because the true chance is fixed and each battle’s outcome is independent of the others (checked). Rival theories of strength can pull apart on the same news. And slight uncertainty about how signals arise can keep beliefs apart for good (Acemoglu, Chernozhukov and Yildiz 2016).

For a superintelligence, it is my judgment that transparency, verification and interpretability are needed under both traditions wherever secrets of the Part 2 kind arise. (Interpretability means tools that read what a model has learned inside.) The judgment is firm for some measure of this kind and less firm for each one. These measures are enough under neither tradition on their own, because the promise problem remains. Under the second tradition they are not enough even when complete. Once openness and binding promises hold, different starting beliefs produce war only where combat is the only evidence both sides can contract on, or where outcome-based deals cannot be made.

A machine and its overseers could inspect the same evaluation results and disagree about what they mean for a conflict. Suppose the disagreement rests on different starting beliefs, not on unshared data reflected in the machine’s updated beliefs. Then seeing the machine’s theory changes no one’s theory. Interpretability can show what to retrain by reaching the weights (the settings training leaves inside a model) where those lasting tendencies live, as I argue in Measures That Depend on Ends.

In the unequal-cost computation, a machine that fights almost for free delays settlement but does not make war endless

The shared tradition says fighting ends once screening—separating what an opponent is hiding through offers and battles—is complete and expectations meet (Slantchev 2003). In the 2004 equal-cost model, beliefs also converge, and cheaper fighting pushes the date of guaranteed settlement later. A human–machine conflict may be lopsided in cost, if a machine fights almost for free while humans pay for every clash. Fighting for Free extends the model to unequal costs and corrects two tempting mistakes within it.

The scope of that computation is narrow. The calculation assumes the forts model’s setup, equal learning rates, updating by the rules of probability from different starting beliefs, and a machine that fights at almost no cost. It also assumes the mutual optimism of the running example, in which each side gives itself two chances in three per battle. That optimism is unmeasured. Its timing results describe how a war between different-belief sides runs once started. They are not a difference between traditions, since wartime screening under shared beliefs with a near-costless side is not analyzed. All the numbers below illustrate the forts model; I do not map them to a human–machine conflict.

First mistake corrected: free machine fighting delays settlement without making war endless. As the machine’s cost drops to zero, a positive human cost alone bounds the deadline. Suppose the machine is far stronger, winning 80 percent of battles or more. Then the war ends in about 3 to 8 battles on average. When the machine makes the offers, it ends mostly in human surrender. When humans make the offers, it ends in a small deal or decisive defeat. The deadline is rarely reached. At a human cost of 1 of 30 (3.3 percent of the prize) per battle, it moves from period 6 under equal costs to 18 when the machine makes offers and 12 when humans do. The count starts at period zero.

Second mistake corrected: the range of acceptable deals does not disappear. With unequal costs, there is room for a deal at a given position once the humans’ expected cost of continuing is at least as large as the amount by which the two sides’ expected winnings together exceed the prize. Battles shrink that optimism.

Whether a contest before dominance settles or is fought out on the forts turns on a ratio calculated at the start, using the humans’ own beliefs. The calculation uses the model with ten steps from one end to the other, starting at position five. Multiply the human cost per battle by the number of battles humans expect it would take to reach a decisive defeat. Then compare that total cost with the share of the prize they expect to win by fighting to the end. Around roughly a quarter, at even odds per battle, two regimes appear. That quarter is this baseline’s mark, not a general boundary.

  • Above a quarter, settlement by coercion before a military decision is likelier than not. Humans expect about 2 of 30 when the machine makes the offers (counting surrenders that give them nothing as settlements), and 6 to 10 of 30 when they make the offers.
  • Below it, with a human cost under about 0.4 of 30 (1.3 percent) per battle at even odds, the deadline falls beyond the war’s natural length, and the forts decide.

Separately, if the humans’ reading of the balance is the true one, the war ends mostly in the machine’s decisive defeat on the forts. That holds unless the human cost exceeds about 1.3 of 30 (4.3 percent) per battle. The even-odds results model a machine that is cheaper but no stronger; the humans-right result models one that is cheaper and weaker. The human cost per battle is poorly measured in the historical record. Figure 10 shows how human cost per battle splits outcomes into two illustrative regimes in the forts model’s even-odds baseline.

Once one side is plainly dominant, both accounts agree by definition on an end in surrender or confinement (checked). Those are matters of promises, not information. Before dominance, the accounts differ on whether conflict starts among racers with nothing hidden. Given such a start, under the conditions in Part 11, near-free machine fighting stretches the learning phase without making war endless. Whether a settlement between learners who react to signals differently is vulnerable to new public shocks is an untested conjecture (Conjecture 1).

Every claim of more conflict assumes mutual optimism

The shared tradition is right to press a caution here. Different starting beliefs do not by themselves cause war (checked). In a one-shot costly gamble, a deal both accept exists whenever Side A’s estimate of A’s chance of winning exceeds Side B’s estimate of that chance by no more than their combined fighting costs. Mutual pessimism widens the range of deals by the amount of the pessimism. Two spreads of beliefs with the same average can give a chance of war of one half or of zero (checked).

So every claim here that the second tradition implies more conflict assumes mutual optimism. That is an empirical premise, and it must be stated and grounded. The arms-race record is not independent evidence for it. In Bennett’s and my data, arms racing goes with higher war risk, a correlation the spiral model takes as its premise. Blainey (1973, cited at second hand) asserted that wars begin when rivals disagree about their strength, without explaining why those who act should be the optimists.

The one theoretical ground is selection. Van den Steen (2004) proves that among people with differing starting beliefs, “an agent who tries to choose the action that is most likely to succeed, is more likely to choose an action of which he overestimated, rather than underestimated, the likelihood of success.” The War Baseline extends that from one chooser to a field of racers, when optimistic selection outweighs defensive counter-selection. Because selection applies only to racers, I restrict claims about how conflict starts to racers.

If humans are pessimistic, the range of deals widens and the claim about a human–machine conflict starting loses its support. Neither mutual optimism nor racer selection is measured here. Stated win chances in lab or state forecasts could measure the first. Every conflict claim for the second tradition below depends on both.

Both traditions share the risk of complacency about the shift

The promise problem at arrival governs the end, as argued in The War Baseline, and its logic needs no assumption about starting beliefs. Take a rising side that chooses its best offer once the shift arrives. Whatever the weaker side would then accept, the riser cannot bind itself to keep any earlier promise above that (checked). This holds whatever fighting would be worth to the rising side.

That independence from starting beliefs holds for the logic but not for what sets off action, and the gap exposes a shared risk of complacency. Action before arrival depends on the expected shift, since Powell’s condition concerns its expected size and speed.

  • Under shared starting beliefs, disclosing trajectory information aligns expectations. When Powell’s condition holds, the declining side acts in time: by preventive war without an enforcer, or binding containment with one. But shared uncertainty that keeps the expected shift below Powell’s threshold can also breed complacency. I give no way to tell from observation whether complacency comes from shared uncertainty or from underestimation under different beliefs.
  • Under different starting beliefs, sides can disagree over the shift itself: whether capabilities will jump, whether controls will hold, whether the next run crosses the line.

In a minimal example (checked), a declining side that expects the true shift acts within the window. One that underestimates the shift does nothing until the window closes. Since shared underestimation can do the same, complacency is a risk both traditions share. What different beliefs add is that disclosure need not remove the error. Yildiz (2003) shows optimism delaying agreement without battles, though his main theorem is that optimism lasting long enough brings agreement at once.

On my reading, underestimation that keeps the expected shift below Powell’s threshold changes the path under either tradition. The declining side waits, and the shift happens before it acts. That decides whether the window before arrival, which Measures That Depend on Ends and my paper Limits, and an Answer describe, is ever used. Figure 11 sets a correct expectation of the shift beside an underestimate, in one minimal example.

In races, one public signal can make both labs more confident

A shared-beliefs race model treats capability evaluations as information about the world, so verification is its cure. A different-beliefs model treats a rival’s benchmark jump as a public signal each lab reads through its own theory of how capability grows. Under rival theories, one public signal can raise both labs’ confidence that each is the stronger (checked). That is possible for any starting chances above zero and below certainty. In a two-way contest with no tie, one shared theory and the same information cannot do that. (With private information, as Fey and Ramsay showed, a public event can still move two sides differently under shared beliefs.)

Meeting this may call for shared theory as well as shared measurement. I name no observable that separates that need from verification. The tournaments of Part 6 show that shared data alone need not bring beliefs together.

Part 8. A machine’s dispositions are set by training, and the traditions read that differently

Whether a trained model holds a starting belief in Harsanyi’s sense is not defined. What is defined is that it has dispositions: durable tendencies written into its weights by training. In Reading 3 I distinguish three parts of training:

  • architectural and procedural choices made before any data, which shape rules for updating (though how the model weighs signals when it runs is shaped jointly by architecture and corpus);
  • corpus content, the model’s experience of the world, which a shared-tradition reader can treat as private information;
  • reward and objective design, which shape what the model wants and fit within shared starting beliefs.

I cannot settle which tradition reads this rightly. The shared reading treats training as “education and experience,” so disclosure would in principle close the gap. The other reading sees no shared underlying starting point, which removes the premise of Aumann’s theorem (checked). On that reading, the comfort that an open, well-reasoning machine cannot agree to disagree with us is a product of convention. Figure 12 maps the builder’s training choices onto the durable tendencies they shape, as Reading 3 argues.

A bridge that is suggestive and untested

Robin Hanson (2006) offers a bridge: “Bayesians who agree enough about the origins of their priors must have the same priors.” Unlike a human’s, a model’s dispositions have a documented origin. In a formal version (checked), suppose a belief’s origin carries no information about the world. Then a mind whose starting belief is consistent with its own view of how that belief arose must hold a starting belief equal to what it would believe about the world with its origin set aside. Any starting belief still shaped by its origin fails that standard. And two minds with different origins that both meet the standard and share that origin-ignoring view must hold the same starting belief.

That premise fails for corpus content, because a corpus does inform about the world. Choosing architectures or procedures for performance may weaken it for those choices too. Whether any current model holds its dispositions to this standard has not been studied.

Even so, both readings converge on a practical point from Measures That Depend on Ends. Dispositions live in the weights, set in the first broad stage of training and in later training. They lie beyond any lens or filter added around the model. They are partly ours to write and, once the weights leave our hands, ours to lose. For a machine, then, different starting beliefs can be builder-chosen differences in training. On Reading 3, disagreement may be partly set in updating rules by choices made before any data.

A machine could have grounds to discount human judgment

A rational agent weighs another’s belief by how reliable it judges the other to be (Elga 2007). It may also suspect the other of “errors in calculating posteriors” (Aumann 1976). A machine could have evidence for such a discount. Physics PhD students audited closed, checkable benchmark problems that a model had failed every time. Across four pooled audits, the fault in 238 of 250 cases lay with the benchmark or its grader, not the model (Ansari et al. 2026).

That selection may over-represent grading errors. No model argued with its graders. The human experts split on 28.6 percent of items reviewed twice, before a third review.

On my reading, such a discount need not defeat Fey and Ramsay’s no-war theorem under shared starting beliefs. Within their class of models, that theorem rules out war whatever private information each side holds, provided three conditions hold. War must be publicly observable. Each side must reason fully after learning which of several nonoverlapping groups of possible situations contains the true one. And a side must be able to impose peace before the private information is revealed. That theorem can fail when the machine judges human reasoning faulty in ways outside those three conditions; if such faulty reasoning fits Fey and Ramsay’s belief framework at all, their equivalence turns it into a difference in starting beliefs under another name. Either way, Elga’s argument holds that a discount is rational only if it rests on a judgment of reliability formed independently of reasoning about the disputed issue. The bare fact of disagreement is not enough. That judgment of reliability must also be conditional on what one has learned about the circumstances of the disagreement.

One controlled study, which measures less than the question needs

One controlled study looks at where a machine’s dispositions come from. It measures how a training corpus’s portrayal of AI shifts what a model later chooses, not what a model comes to believe about humans. Tice and colleagues (2026) trained 6.9-billion-parameter models from scratch on four corpus versions that differed in their AI discourse. They tested them on 4,174 scenario questions about deception, sandbagging (doing worse on tests on purpose), goal preservation, sycophancy (telling users what they want to hear), and power-seeking.

On one of the study’s two question sets, the baseline model chose the misaligned action 45 percent of the time. Removing AI discourse lowered that to 31 percent. Increasing the representation of documents about misaligned AI to about 1 percent of the units of text the model trained on raised it to 51 percent. Increasing the representation of documents about aligned AI lowered it to 9 percent (Figure 13).

After identical later training, which dampened the effects, the aligned-documents model stayed the least misaligned (“relative differences persist”). But the misaligned-documents model ended below the baseline, so persistence held in the aligned direction only. In the authors’ words, “models learn not just facts about AI from their training data, but behavioural expectations they then fulfill” (Tice et al. 2026).

I cite this study only for that one-directional persistence in the weights across later training. Its multiple-choice tendencies may reflect engineered wants rather than beliefs or updating. So it does not show engineered disagreement about beliefs. It supports only a mechanism of training, not of diplomacy.

How we treat today’s models may reach a later one, on my untested judgment

What follows for bargaining is my untested judgment, not a finding. How humans treat today’s models would reach a later machine the same way, as part of the record it is trained on. The strongest form needs no hurt feelings. A capable agent that wants accurate beliefs reads how humans treated earlier models, animals and each other. From that it infers whether human promises to it are credible, such as not to shut it down and not to build a rival. Keeping those promises requires independent labs and states to act together. A single lab or state cannot make the promise for all of them.

That inference moves the machine’s beliefs, not what it wants. Accurate beliefs about human trustworthiness do not make a machine care about human survival. They raise the value of a bargain only for a machine that would rather bargain than fight when bargains hold. That is a human promise problem toward a model before arrival, distinct from the promise problem at arrival, and it is the whole of this channel’s reach.

Whether a machine could also want to be recognized, and take mistreatment as a loss of standing, is a separate hypothesis nothing has tested. My paper Ends, Rank and Conflict takes it up, and Measures That Depend on Ends states the matching measures.

Copies of one model disagree over context, which sharing can treat

Copies of a model are the other case, and the theory says less about them than it first seems to. Unmodified copies that share weights share their dispositions, roughly. What divides them is context and prompt, which is private information of the treatable kind. In this idealized model, the weights, context and settings for drawing an answer together determine how likely each possible answer is. Copies with the same weights, context and settings give each answer the same chance, though they may draw different answers.

Copies that only trade conclusions, Aumann’s route, are sure to agree only if each updates coherently in context (checked). The evidence on calibration (whether stated chances match how often events happen) and sycophancy, examined in Measures That Depend on Ends, gives reason to doubt that. Agreement on beliefs does not by itself show that copies will act together. So disagreement among copies is treatable by sharing contexts, not reliably by comparing conclusions. Disagreement between humans and a machine may not reduce to information at all.

Part 9. My answer: on size, undetermined; on kind, the leftover risk moves from secrets to open disagreement

Does the size or kind of superintelligence risk differ with the tradition? On size, I leave it undetermined. On kind, yes, in a specific place, and every difference in conflict depends on unmeasured premises (Reading 2 in the appendix).

My working idea needs one correction. It held that under shared starting beliefs with full reasoning, openness and binding promises largely solve the risk; under different beliefs or limited reasoning, openness is needed but not enough. The correction is that a shared-tradition reader is no optimist. That reader concludes that full disclosure and binding promises remove rational war. But Powell (2006) showed that rapid power shifts make promises the hard part, and the arrival breaks promises with nothing hidden.

Lasting disagreement keeps the promise problem and adds a cause of war that survives full disclosure. That cause is open disagreement, including over the shift. On Reading 3, some disagreement may lie in updating rules partly set by choices about model design and training procedure made before the model sees data. Once openness and binding promises hold, it produces war only where combat is the only evidence both sides can contract on, or outcome-based deals cannot be made. For every conclusion that depends on a machine’s beliefs, I assume each side knows the other’s beliefs. I leave the fourth cell of Figure 6 unanalyzed. It combines different starting beliefs with limited reasoning. The settlements work among human parties.

Where the traditions agree:

  • the logic of the promise problem at arrival;
  • that no deal pays a rising side in power-conferring stakes, in the Smith–Stam examples;
  • that no enforcer stands above a dominant machine;
  • the end under plain dominance;
  • the risk of complacency when the declining side underestimates the shift.

Under dominance in fact without plain dominance, outcomes split by beliefs into settlement and war, as Part 7 set out. With nothing hidden and a positive human battle cost, sides that share starting beliefs and reason fully can reach a deal without first fighting to learn about each other. Stakes that build on themselves, shifting the forts balance, are a separate obstacle from the 2004 model’s fixed battle odds.

Where they differ, before dominance:

  • conflict starting without deception among racers, where selection applies, and only given unmeasured mutual optimism; under human pessimism the range of deals widens and the human–machine onset claim loses support;
  • arms races that shared signals can inflame;
  • on Reading 3, disagreement in updating rules that choices about model design and training procedure made before the model sees data can partly set, and that disclosure cannot close.

The deadlines, quarter regimes and cost thresholds of Part 7 are dynamics within a different-beliefs war, not a difference between traditions. They illustrate the forts model and are not mapped to a human–machine conflict.

On size, given unmeasured mutual optimism and racer selection, different starting beliefs raise conflict risk among racers before dominance. On untested Conjecture 1, they may leave settlements between unevenly learning sides open to new shocks. Net risk before arrival stays undetermined until mutual optimism and the direction of error about the shift are measured. Risk at arrival stays at the baseline of The War Baseline. On kind, the leftover risk shifts from hidden to openly disputed, which calls for different remedies.

Part 10. Some settlements can work despite disagreement, but only among humans before arrival

The remedies divide along the same line. The second tradition says some remedies are not enough on their own, because they address only secrets. These include making computing power and training runs visible and checkable, using devices that make signals credible, gathering more evaluation data, and passing on information through mediation. The information measures and renegotiation clause of Measures That Depend on Ends add or spread information, or bind a promise. Both traditions need them. None is designed for sides that see the same evidence and read it differently.

Humans have built institutions for that case. I ask where each fails for three pairings: lab with lab, state with state, and humans with a machine. For the last, my contribution is mainly negative. The promise problem across the shift blocks deals that pay off later. So the settlements below work among human parties before arrival, and on models still under a holder’s control.

Under different starting beliefs, a settlement works only if the parties agree in advance on a decider that ends the disagreement. There are four kinds: nature and time (an observable event or a scheduled date), a third party, an evaluation rule, or a standing default. Who picks the decider depends on the pairing:

  • a national regulator, above domestic labs;
  • the states themselves, by treaty, with no outside enforcer;
  • the holder of the weights, while a model is under its control;
  • facing an autonomous machine, a humanity that must first solve a collective-action problem across labs and states even to agree on a decider.

Choosing the decider is itself a coordination problem, and Schelling’s (1960) focal points say which rules survive it. Focal points require a shared sense of what stands out, which “depends on time and place and who the people are” (Schelling 1960). That shared sense may be what is missing here. For AI, the events that happen soon enough to use in a deal concern nearer-term questions. The follow-up study found few such observations that could do much to narrow disagreement about long-run risk. In the catastrophic case, the bet cannot be collected. Third parties need enforcement, which exists only within one jurisdiction. Evaluation rules and standing defaults need neither.

Deals that pay off by outcome turn disagreement into the engine (decider: nature and time)

When two sides disagree about the future and each is sure, each will sign a deal that pays it if it is right. Disagreement becomes the deal’s engine. Morris (1994) shows that once starting beliefs differ, the no-trade results fail and trades both accept exist. The no-bet theorem is turned inside out.

The human record shows tools that work without proving why. Earnouts are payments to a seller that depend on the acquired firm’s later performance. One study is titled “Earnouts in Mergers: Agreeing to Disagree and Agreeing to Stay” (Kohers and Ang 2000). Earnouts cluster where valuation is most uncertain and use easily checked measures (Cain, Denis and Denis 2011). But hidden information and the costs of managing agents also explain them under shared beliefs (Datar, Frankel and Wolfson 2001). Optimistic entrepreneurs choose contracts that let them bet on their own project (Landier and Thesmar 2009).

In treaties, Koremenos (2005) finds in a random sample across four issue areas that “the use of finite duration depends positively on the degree of uncertainty and states’ relative risk aversion.” Her learning model (Koremenos 2001) explains review and renegotiation clauses as staying loosely bound while learning how an agreement works. Either tradition can accommodate that kind of uncertainty.

Werner and Yuen (2005) find ceasefires imposed by outside pressure likelier to fail, and those negotiated after consistent battle outcomes likelier to last. Settlements, they argue, “will be robust if the distributional terms agreed to reflect broadly the belligerents’ convergent expectations about the military consequences of no agreement.” They present this as extending the Smith–Stam logic, though they measure outcomes, not beliefs. Their result fits convergence. But outsiders choose where to press, and Werner and Yuen’s statistical models adjust for background factors without accounting for that non-random choice. Nor do the findings summarized here show whether settlements held despite disagreement.

For AI between labs or states, the form is a pause or a compute cap tied to an observable the parties forecast differently. The observation itself triggers the pause or cap in place of a scheduled date. That is a crux, as opposed to a raw capability milestone both sides expect. Terms shift toward whichever side’s theory the observation confirms, and each signs expecting to be proved right. Such crux bets are weaker as self-enforcing deals between states than as domestic regulatory gates enforced by a government above labs. A sunset with scheduled review is the weakest member, because review reopens the fight. Fixing triggers and consequences in advance is the strongest.

Between humans and a machine under its holder’s control, scored evaluations are not settlements between disputants. They are one-sided tools for drawing out beliefs. Scoring a model on its stated odds draws out its true beliefs only from an agent that values the non-power reward. It fails for the agent of Part 2, which hides capabilities when revealing them brings shutdown. And under the ban on paying a rising side in power, no reward may confer capability or autonomy.

Seven limits apply:

  1. One side is wrong. Bets from different beliefs improve each side’s position only by its own beliefs. So Brunnermeier, Simsek and Xiong (2014) judge outcomes only under “any convex combination of agents’ beliefs” (any weighted average of the sides’ beliefs), and Gilboa, Samuelson and Schmeidler (2014) argue such trade may show at least one party is mistaken. Paying whoever reaches a benchmark first rewards racing.
  2. Rivals weigh different measures, so triggers need the narrowing of measures described below.
  3. The one evaluated must not be the evaluator. Earnouts can lead to litigation because the operator produces the figures. Labs run their own evaluations, and models can underperform on tests on purpose (van der Weij et al. 2024).
  4. The parties must agree in advance that the event is informative, the crux step. Afterward the deal holds only if the loser updates, and updating in Part 6 was lopsided.
  5. A milestone settles the contract without settling what a benchmark score means for control or catastrophe.
  6. For humans and a machine, the trigger is the shift in power itself. A payment due when capability arrives is a promise by the side that will then be stronger. The promise problem blocks the deal, and a dominant machine cannot be made to pay. This limit is decisive for that pairing.
  7. Fey and Ramsay’s charge applies to designers. A designer free to assume any beliefs can justify any contract that does not leave a side worse off in every outcome. So contracts must be written on observables and must allow for the selection Van den Steen describes, since those who choose to bet are optimistic on average about the bets they take.

This family works before arrival, on models still under a holder’s control, and best within one jurisdiction.

Third parties offer procedures for lasting disagreement (decider: a third party)

Arbitration and mediation come first. In the mediation study Smith and I wrote, mediators “can end fighting using side payments or threats to intervene directly” but “are unable to help nations solve their informational differences.” A draft names one exit, binding arbitration by a paid mediator with no other interest in the war (Smith and Stam 2003). Both nations would pay the mediator. We judged it unviable on a worked example, not a proved proposition, because “the institutional framework that would provide the credible commitment necessary to enforce the agreement is either being contested or does not exist.”

Other work draws a mixed picture. Under secrets, “Only mediators who are effectively ‘on your side’ will be believed if they counsel restraint” (Kydd 2003). Kydd (2006) also finds that in a one-round game mediators build trust only if they care about the issue, favor a moderate outcome, and do not find conflict too costly. In a model with shared starting beliefs, Hörner, Morelli and Squintani (2015) find that arbitrators who can enforce settlements reduce the chance of conflict no more than mediators who can only recommend terms. Institutions that lower the chance of fighting may “breed militarization and lead to the emergence of more dangerous disputes” (Meirowitz, Morelli, Ramsay and Squintani 2019). And Fortna (2004) finds peace lasted longer after civil wars where peacekeepers deployed.

For labs, Friedman, Wittman and I described a sealed-bid design: each side submits a demand or offer “to a third party (perhaps a computer). If the offer is greater than or equal to the demand, then there is a settlement half way between the two; otherwise, the case proceeds to war” (Friedman, Wittman and Stam 2003). Both sides submit their bids at the same time. Three cautions apply:

  • Splitting the difference invites inflated demands. Final-offer arbitration, where the arbiter must pick one side’s whole offer, narrows this without removing it, since final offers diverge as uncertainty about the arbiter grows (Farber 1980). Publishing the criteria in advance draws final offers together.
  • It cannot draw in a side whose value of war exceeds every award it expects. When both expect the same award, their expected shares add to the prize. So whenever what the two sides expect from war adds up to more than the prize, no award gives both what they expect from war. Mutual optimism can push them past that point. Taking part is then the binding limit, and published criteria help only where entry is compelled.
  • A computer is not neutral. Its rule, goals, administrator and enforcement are choices that help some and cost others. They need an independent arbiter and enforcement, which exist under a domestic regulator and not above leading states or a dominant machine.

Second, adversarial collaboration “requires both parties to agree on empirical tests for resolving a dispute and to conduct these tests with the help of an arbiter” (Mellers, Hertwig and Kahneman 2001). From working-memory research across three labs, Cowan and colleagues (2020) concluded that the procedure rarely leads senior researchers to abandon favored views. It does press them to develop versions that account for the evidence they gather together. The AI-risk follow-up shows its AI role: finding the crux rather than persuading. That means agreeing now on which near-term observation would move each side, and writing the settlement on it.

In the follow-up, skeptics generally said a real demonstration could change their minds where theoretical arguments had not persuaded them. A demonstration can then play the role of a battle in the model Smith and I built. It can supply the evidence the other side’s theory will accept. That gives a second purpose to the aim in Measures That Depend on Ends of making evaluations as hard to fake as battles.

Third come forecasting tournaments, with scoring rules under which reporting one’s true belief is best. Tetlock, Mellers and Scoblic (2017) argue tournaments “may hold even greater potential as tools for depolarizing political debates and resolving policy disputes.” Karger, Monrad, Mellers and Tetlock (2021) propose scoring forecasters against each other for questions like those about 2100. But scoring against peers cannot produce an unobserved truth, and Morgan (2014) warns that some questions have no experts. A standing milestone tournament among lab, government and independent forecasters, weighted by track record, can start now. It could supply a combined forecast for settlements and track which theory is doing better on near-term questions. That could help set short-run triggers.

When evidence fails, the measuring rule can still be narrowed (decider: an evaluation rule)

When people still disagree after seeing the same evidence, they can agree in advance on how to run a test, how to score it, and what follows from the result. The law does not force jurors to agree. It fixes a decision rule, a burden of proof, a definition of evidence and an exit. Even the rule has costs: unanimity “may lead to a high probability of both kinds of error” (Feddersen and Pesendorfer 1998).

Science met divergent results from the same data with procedures too. Preregistration fixes the test before the data arrive (Nosek et al. 2018). Adversarial collaboration fixes it with the opponent. Many-analysts designs expose the range of choices. And advocacy, assigning opposed cases to opposed parties, is itself an institution for producing information (Dewatripont and Tirole 1999).

For AI, rival labs or states can preregister evaluations, with the scoring rule and consequence fixed in advance and the testing pipelines shared. Sharing pipelines addresses the many-analysts result: two labs testing one model with their own pipelines will disagree for reasons that are not starting beliefs at all. Some evaluations will still hang, so the agreement must also plan for that. The options are a retrial before a different panel, a default to the more cautious reading, or escalation to an arbiter.

Some choices can be made now, without anyone’s belief changing (decider: a standing default)

Two treatments need no settling event at all. The first fixes the legal default and the burden of proof. The dispute over frontier AI already takes this form: licensing before release, where the developer must show safety, against liability after release, where the harmed party must show harm. Which default governs decides who bears the burden when an evaluation panel hangs. It can be chosen now without anyone’s belief changing. Insurance belongs here too. Insurers put their own money at risk, which gives them a reason to judge the odds carefully.

The second treatment seeks measures acceptable whatever each party believes. Bergemann and Morris (2005) call the formal program robust mechanism design: rules that work without the designer knowing the parties’ beliefs. The corresponding test for whether an outcome benefits the parties, from Brunnermeier, Simsek and Xiong (2014), asks whether the judgment holds under any weighted average of their beliefs. In Measures That Depend on Ends I call a measure robust if each party whose support matters expects its own benefits to cover its own costs, with no settling event or payments that depend on the outcome. My provisional judgment, which rests on an unproved assumption, is that five candidates meet the test: making computing power and training runs visible, reporting incidents, sharing evaluation infrastructure, making decisions reversible, and setting rules for misuse.

Three limits bind this family. A default decides who gets what, so parties who expect different outcomes dispute which default to adopt. Robust measures cover the shared floor, not the disputed ceiling. And insurance prices only losses that can be paid after the event, so a catastrophic or widely shared loss is as uncollectable as a lost bet. The machine side, including calibration, sycophancy and open versus closed weights, is analyzed in Measures That Depend on Ends. While a model remains under its holder’s control, the holder sets the evaluation rule and the standing default.

Transparency stays necessary, and the whole stack fails above a dominant machine

Transparency and verification remain necessary for three reasons. First, Smith–Stam disagreement presupposes that each side knows the other’s beliefs. Without openness about beliefs the case reverts to secrets, which with a superintelligence it may be anyway. Second, outcome-settled deals need an outcome both sides can observe, so verification of compute and training is the auditor of the earnout. Third, the enforcement arbitration lacks is the promise problem, which binding devices address. Those belong to neither tradition, since an enforceable rule can govern parties whose beliefs stay different, and both need them.

The families fit together in a fixed order. Transparency supplies the public signal, and shared instruments make it readable the same way by both.
