Outcome-settled deals then turn the remaining disagreement into a payoff instead of a fight. Procedures with decision rules act when the trigger itself is disputed. Defaults and robust measures act when nothing settles. Honest machine reporting makes the machine’s odds a usable input, and binding devices hold the result. Figure 14 shows how these settlements fit together among human parties, and where the whole stack fails.

In my judgment, ranked by risk covered and near-term feasibility, the order runs as follows:

  1. Preregistered joint evaluations with crux-triggered consequences, alongside robust measures and defaults, which need no settling event. Triggers must be observables the parties forecast differently, not raw milestones both expect. Because near-term cruxes are thin, defaults share the top rank to govern the gap that does not close. Defaults work under either tradition, while crux triggers use disagreement and are weaker between states than at home.
  2. Training models to report honest uncertainty, as a precondition rather than a settlement. In my judgment its feasibility is medium rather than high, because fixing benchmark scoring is a collective-action problem across racing labs.
  3. Standing scored forecasting comes next as the low-cost tool, followed by arbitration where a government stands above the parties. Last comes research into ways to read a machine’s beliefs from the model.

The whole stack fails where everything else fails. Above a dominant machine there is no one to hold the stakes, no arbiter and no enforcer, and a lost bet cannot be collected. Every treatment is strongest between labs under one government, weaker between states, and absent after arrival. That gives a second reason, alongside the one in The War Baseline, why the years before a dominant machine matter most.

Part 11. What I have not modelled, not measured, or not claimed, and what would change my answer

Seven things are not modelled

  1. Lopsided learning between sides that react to signals differently is shown only as a two-date possibility, not solved as a game over time. The window example before arrival covers only a declining side that underestimates the shift, not one that overestimates it.
  2. Wartime screening under shared starting beliefs with a near-costless side is not analyzed. So the finite deadline, the sizing of the range of deals by human cost, and the shock sensitivity of an early settlement all assume updating from different starting beliefs. They depend on the mutual optimism built into the running example.
  3. The unequal-cost forts model assumes fixed battle odds, a loser who survives (ruling out physical elimination by construction), pauses for bargaining after each clash, and near-zero machine fighting cost. None of these is established for any human–machine contest.
  4. The baseline treats humanity as one side. In fact, divisions among labs, states and publics make human promises and the choice of decider collective-action problems.
  5. The fourth combination, different starting beliefs with limited reasoning, is left unanalyzed.
  6. The irreversible release of model weights is treated in Measures That Depend on Ends, not modelled here.
  7. A human–machine encounter may fall in that fourth combination. For every conclusion that depends on a machine’s beliefs, I assume each side knows the other’s beliefs. Those conclusions are not shown for the fourth combination. The settlements work among human parties.

Four quantities are not measured

  1. The human cost per battle in a human–machine conflict. It sets the deadline and separates the two illustrative regimes. The historical record measures it badly. Writing about the costs in Bueno de Mesquita and Lalman’s model of war, Signorino (1999) called such data “difficult, if not impossible, to obtain.”
  2. Whether any model holds its dispositions to Hanson’s standard and corrects for training choices made before data, while sharing an origin-ignoring belief. This has not been studied. Corpus content informs about the world, and choosing architectures for performance may weaken the premise for those choices too.
  3. Whether training shifts a model’s beliefs about humans, or about who would prevail in a conflict. No study cited here measures it. Tice and colleagues (2026) used small models and synthetic documents. They varied how AI is portrayed, not how AI is treated, measured no restraint by a capable system, and recorded multiple-choice tendencies that may reflect wants rather than beliefs or real behavior. A July 2025 dissent, known to me at second hand, judges the initial training stage a smaller influence than later training (AI Futures Project 2025). It judges that a model is unlikely to behave very differently in practice because of what the earlier training led it to expect, unless those portrayals stand out strongly and later training does little to counter the effect.
  4. Mutual optimism. Every claim of more conflict under different starting beliefs depends on it. Its only ground here is the stated, unmeasured condition for extending Van den Steen’s selection result to racers, which does not cover a declining side and limits the onset claims to racers.

In addition, neither forecasting tournament met Aumann’s conditions.

Three claims are not made, and several steps are judgments

I do not claim that any record of behavior refutes shared starting beliefs with full reasoning. Nor do I claim that either tradition’s reading of model training is uniquely right. And I do not claim the traditions differ on the end once one side is plainly dominant.

Several steps are judgments or conjectures:

  • my judgment that transparency, verification and interpretability are needed under both traditions wherever secrets arise (firm for some measure, less firm for each);
  • my reading of how the Fey–Ramsay debate bears on rivals, or a machine, with no enforcer above them;
  • my judgment that underestimating the shift can breed complacency under either tradition;
  • Hanson’s “suggestive and untested” bridge, and my untested judgment that how we treat current models shapes a later machine’s view of human promises;
  • my ranking of settlement tools;
  • my untested conjecture that settlements between unevenly learning sides are vulnerable to new public shocks.

What would change the answer

These follow from the open links above:

  • a route to revealing hidden capabilities or goals that is cheaper than transparency, verification or interpretability;
  • evidence that frontier models apply Hanson’s origin correction to training choices made before data;
  • controlled experiments showing that training shifts a model’s beliefs about humans and the balance of power, or that the corpus effect is small;
  • measurement of the human cost per battle; of mutual optimism, for example through stated win chances in lab or state forecasts; of selection against counter-selection among racers; or of how vulnerable settlements are to new shocks when sides learn unevenly;
  • demonstrations in long-range forecasting that structured deliberation and shared indicators close the gap on AI risk.

Part 12. What to take away

A rising superintelligence is the extreme holder of secrets about what it can do and what it wants, and it may also bring open disagreement with nothing hidden. Fey and Ramsay prove, within their class of models, that shared starting beliefs with limited reasoning can be swapped for different starting beliefs with full reasoning. Months of forecasting tournaments on existential risk fit lasting disagreement but do not rule out shared beliefs with full reasoning.

Both traditions share the risk of complacency when the declining side underestimates the shift. Given plain dominance, they reach by definition the same end under the promise problem. They differ before dominance, and on what remains after openness and binding promises: nothing, or lasting disagreement. Under the conditions in Parts 9 and 11, racers who inspect the same evaluations and know each other’s beliefs can still fight without secrets. They can inflame races through shared signals. And on Reading 3 they can face disagreement in updating rules that choices about model design and training procedure made before the model sees data may partly set.

Every conclusion that depends on a machine’s beliefs assumes each side knows the other’s beliefs. I leave the combination of different starting beliefs and limited reasoning unanalyzed. How large the total risk is before arrival remains undetermined. What changes is its kind: the leftover risk moves from secrets to open disagreement. The settlements I analyze for that work among human parties, before a dominant machine arrives.

Where to read more

  • Disagreement Without Hidden Information, the technical paper this guide retells, with the exact setups, the twenty-four checked deductions, the three argued readings and the conjecture in its appendix.
  • The War Baseline: the promise problem at arrival, the arms-race spiral of optimism, racer selection, and the ban on paying a rising side in power, all of which I take as given.
  • Fighting for Free: the summary and correction of the 2004 learning-by-fighting model, and the unequal-cost computation behind the deadlines and regimes in Part 7.
  • Measures That Depend on Ends: the remedies I build on, including robust measures, renegotiation, retraining through the weights, and the evidence on calibration and sycophancy.
  • Ends, Rank and Conflict: the untested hypothesis that a machine might want recognition and take mistreatment as a loss of standing.
  • Limits, and an Answer: the window before arrival whose use, on my reading, complacency can decide.
